questions.scenario: Your company's biggest feature launch in a year just shipped. Two weeks in, the core metric hasn't moved at all.

options.text: Pull the launch data apart segment by segment — the aggregate might be hiding a win in one cohort and a loss in another.
Get on the phone with 10 users who tried it and 10 who didn't. The numbers say 'what' but not 'why.'
Zoom out — is the feature actually serving the right strategic bet, or did we build the right thing for the wrong future?
Check the onboarding and activation flows — if users aren't even discovering the feature properly, the problem is distribution, not the feature itself.

questions.scenario: A senior engineer on your team pushes back hard on a spec you wrote, saying the approach is fundamentally wrong. The team is watching.

options.text: Invite them to write up their alternative approach and schedule time to evaluate both proposals with the team.
Ask them to walk you through the technical concerns in detail — there might be an insight you missed in the constraints.
Reframe the conversation around user outcomes — which approach better solves the core user problem, regardless of technical elegance?
Propose running both approaches as an A/B test — let the data settle the debate rather than opinions.

questions.scenario: You're a new PM at a company. In your first month, you realize the product roadmap has no clear connection to any measurable business outcomes.

options.text: Build a metrics tree connecting company goals to product bets, and use it to start prioritization conversations.
Interview every stakeholder to understand their vision — the roadmap might be disconnected because the strategy itself isn't aligned.
Map the roadmap against the user journey — the missing link might be that we're building features that don't address real user pain points.
Focus on shipping what's already committed quickly and well — earn trust through execution before trying to change the roadmap process.

questions.scenario: Your CEO asks you to present next quarter's product strategy to the board in 48 hours. You have data but no narrative.

options.text: Start with the market shift — frame the strategy as a response to where the world is going, not just what users want today.
Lead with three user stories that make the problem vivid, then connect each to a product bet with clear success criteria.
Build the story around the funnel — show where users are dropping off, what experiments you'll run, and the expected lift.
Structure it as a team capacity plan — what you'll ship, when, and the tradeoffs you're making to hit each milestone.

questions.scenario: Your product has strong retention but new user growth has flatlined for two quarters. The exec team wants answers.

options.text: Audit every acquisition channel — map cost per acquisition, conversion rates, and identify which channels have room to scale.
Talk to churned trial users and people who considered your product but chose a competitor — the answer is in the non-users.
Challenge the assumption that you need new users — maybe the real opportunity is expanding revenue from existing users through upsell and expansion.
Run a rapid series of activation experiments — small changes to onboarding, signup flow, and first-use experience to find quick wins.

questions.scenario: A designer on your team has a radically different vision for a key feature than what engineering scoped. Both have strong arguments.

options.text: Go back to user research — test both concepts with real users and let their reactions break the tie.
Facilitate a structured design review where both present their case and the team votes on criteria you define upfront.
Find the fastest path to testing both — scope down each to an MVP version and A/B test them in production.
Evaluate which version ships faster with fewer dependencies — in the time debating, you could have learned from real usage.

questions.scenario: You're reviewing your product's analytics dashboard and notice a feature you launched 3 months ago has near-zero adoption.

options.text: Set up user sessions to watch people navigate around the feature — if they're not using it, they either can't find it or don't understand its value.
Kill it. Zero adoption after 3 months means the market voted. Reallocate the resources to higher-impact work.
Check the discovery path — maybe the feature works great but it's buried. Test moving it to a prominent position or adding in-app prompts.
Re-examine the original hypothesis — does this feature still align with where we're taking the product, or has the strategy shifted?

questions.scenario: Your team just missed a deadline by two weeks. The CEO is frustrated. Your team is demoralized. You need to address both.

options.text: Run a blameless retro with the team first — understand what broke in the process before communicating anything upward.
Cut scope for the next sprint to rebuild the team's confidence with a quick win, then gradually increase ambition.
Reframe the conversation with the CEO around outcomes, not timelines — show what you learned and how it changes the approach.
Dig into the data on what actually shipped versus what was planned — use it to set more realistic expectations and improve estimation.

questions.scenario: Your biggest competitor just launched a feature that undercuts your core value proposition. Your sales team is panicking. Your CEO wants a response plan by Friday.

options.text: Don't panic-ship a copycat. Double down on what makes you differentiated — competitors can copy features but not your positioning.
Get on calls with 5 at-risk customers this week — understand if this is a real threat or sales noise before making any product moves.
Ship a fast, scrappy response to close the gap — not perfect, but enough to give sales a story while you build the real answer.
Analyze the competitor's distribution strategy — how are they getting this in front of customers? That's often more important than the feature itself.

questions.scenario: You have strong evidence that a beloved feature used by 15% of users is actually hurting conversion for the other 85%. Removing it would be controversial.

options.text: Run a controlled experiment — gradually reduce the feature's prominence and measure the impact on both cohorts before deciding.
Talk to power users first — understand their workflow so deeply that you can build something that serves them without hurting the majority.
Frame this as a strategic choice about who your product is for. If 85% of users are better served without it, the feature is in the wrong product.
Communicate the decision transparently to the team and affected users, with a clear migration path and timeline.

questions.scenario: You're scaling from 3 PMs to 10. The founders want to preserve the 'scrappy startup' culture. You need to add process without killing speed.

options.text: Design lightweight rituals — weekly product reviews, a shared roadmap, and clear ownership areas. Enough structure to coordinate, not enough to suffocate.
Focus on hiring criteria — if you hire PMs who are strong autonomous operators, you need less process. Culture scales through people, not documents.
Build a shared metrics framework first — if every PM team knows their north star and how it connects to the company goal, they can be autonomous.
Write a product strategy doc that's specific enough to enable independent decision-making — the PM equivalent of 'commander's intent.'

questions.scenario: Your freemium product has great adoption but terrible monetization. Only 2% of free users convert to paid. The board is pressuring you to improve unit economics.

options.text: Redesign the free-to-paid boundary — the issue is probably that free users get too much value without hitting a natural upgrade moment.
Interview converted users about their 'aha moment' — then engineer more free users toward that experience.
Set up a conversion funnel experiment — test pricing tiers, feature gates, and upgrade prompts systematically to find the optimal configuration.
Step back and question the model — maybe freemium is wrong for this market. Consider usage-based pricing or a different go-to-market entirely.

questions.scenario: Your product has accumulated significant technical debt. Engineering wants 6 weeks to refactor. Your CEO sees it as 6 weeks without new features.

options.text: Negotiate a hybrid approach — allocate 20% of each sprint to debt while continuing feature work. Sustained investment beats big-bang rewrites.
Quantify the debt in terms the CEO understands — show how it's slowing feature velocity, increasing bugs, and costing the business money.
Reframe the refactor as a strategic investment — connect it to the product vision and explain what it enables that can't be built on the current foundation.
Focus the refactor on the parts that affect users most — page load times, reliability, the things that directly impact retention and satisfaction.

questions.scenario: You're launching in a new market segment. Your data team says the segment looks promising based on TAM analysis, but you have zero direct customer insights.

options.text: Spend two weeks embedded with potential customers before building anything. TAM means nothing if you don't understand the buyer's real workflow.
Build the smallest possible version and launch it with a landing page — real demand is the only data point that matters.
Design a systematic market entry experiment — define success metrics, set a time-boxed learning phase, and commit to a go/no-go decision point.
Map the distribution channels for this segment first — if there's no efficient way to reach these customers, the TAM is irrelevant.

questions.scenario: Two product teams in your organization are building overlapping features. Each team believes their approach is better. Neither wants to give up ownership.

options.text: Reorganize the team boundaries — this is a structural problem that won't be solved by negotiation. Clear ownership prevents future conflicts.
Define the success metric and let the data decide — run both as experiments with clear criteria for which approach wins.
Elevate the decision to the product strategy level — which approach better serves the long-term product vision? Use that as the tiebreaker.
Put both teams in a room with actual users — let the customer perspective dissolve the internal politics.

questions.scenario: Your product is growing 10% month-over-month organically. Leadership asks if you should invest in paid acquisition to accelerate growth.

options.text: Not yet — first understand and amplify the organic growth loops. Paid acquisition on top of a leaky funnel is just burning money faster.
Run a small paid experiment to understand unit economics — if CAC/LTV works, scale it. If not, you've learned cheaply.
Interview your best organic users to understand why they chose you — then build your paid messaging around those authentic reasons.
Invest the budget in making the product better instead — 10% organic growth that compounds is more valuable than paid growth that stops when the budget stops.

questions.scenario: You discover that your most successful product decision was built on flawed data. The feature works, users love it, but the original rationale was wrong. Leadership doesn't know.

options.text: Fix the data pipeline and disclose the error to leadership. Then reframe the success around the real 'why' — rebuilding credibility on accurate foundations matters more than looking good.
Conduct user research to understand the actual reason the feature works — the data was wrong, but the instinct was right. Find the real story.
Use this as a leadership moment — share the mistake with your team to build a culture where intellectual honesty is valued over being right.
The feature works and users love it. Focus forward — use this as a lesson about the limits of data-driven decisions, but don't let it paralyze future bets.

questions.scenario: You've been promoted to lead the company's most important product area. On day one, you realize the team is deeply dysfunctional — low trust, unclear roles, and a backlog of broken promises to customers.

options.text: Start with 1:1s with every team member and key stakeholders. Understand the history before changing anything — trust is rebuilt through listening, not restructuring.
Pick one broken promise to customers, fix it fast and visibly. Quick wins rebuild credibility with both the team and customers simultaneously.
Write and share a clear product vision for the next 12 months. Dysfunction often stems from lack of direction — give people something to rally around.
Set up a clean data baseline — define metrics, instrument tracking, and establish weekly reviews. You can't fix what you can't measure.

questions.scenario: Your product has achieved strong product-market fit in your initial market. The CEO wants to expand to enterprise. This would require significant changes to the product, team, and go-to-market.

options.text: Build a separate enterprise team that can move fast without disrupting the core product. Two-in-a-box: one team protects what works, another explores.
Start with the go-to-market motion, not the product — sign 5 design partners, sell what you have, and let their feedback tell you what to build.
Map the enterprise user journey end-to-end — admin provisioning, SSO, audit logs. The product gaps aren't features, they're infrastructure.
Challenge the premise — does enterprise expansion align with your long-term vision, or is it a distraction? Not every company should go upmarket.

questions.scenario: You're building an AI-powered feature that could 10x the product's value. But it's unpredictable — sometimes brilliant, sometimes embarrassingly wrong. Your brand reputation is on the line.

options.text: Ship it as a 'beta' or 'experimental' feature with clear guardrails. Set user expectations explicitly and collect feedback to improve rapidly.
Design the UX to be transparent about AI confidence levels — let users see when the system is sure vs. guessing. Trust comes from honesty, not perfection.
Build a rigorous evaluation framework — define accuracy thresholds, automate regression testing, and only ship when the model meets your quality bar.
Ship it boldly. The window for AI differentiation is narrow — being first matters more than being perfect. Your competitors won't wait.

questions.scenario: You realize your product has become a 'feature factory' — shipping lots of things but none of them are moving the needle. The team is busy but impact is flat.

options.text: Halt the roadmap and rewrite the strategy from scratch. Align every initiative to 2-3 big bets that could fundamentally change the trajectory.
Implement an impact review — for every feature shipped in the last 6 months, measure the actual outcome. Let the data show the team what's working and what isn't.
Go spend a week in the field with customers. The disconnect between shipping and impact usually means you've lost touch with what users actually need.
Change the team structure — move from feature teams to outcome teams. When teams own metrics instead of features, they naturally focus on impact.

questions.scenario: You're offered a once-in-a-career opportunity to build a new product from zero at your company. But it means leaving your current team, which you've spent two years building and is finally hitting its stride.

options.text: Take it — but only after ensuring a strong successor is in place and a transition plan protects the team's momentum. Leaders are measured by what thrives after they leave.
Take it — zero-to-one is where the most learning and impact happens. Your current team is strong enough to continue without you, and that's a sign of success.
Before deciding, deeply understand the new product's users and market. Zero-to-one only works if you're building for a real problem. Validate first.
Negotiate to run both for 3 months — prototype the new product while winding down your current role. Test the opportunity before committing fully.

questions.scenario: Your company is going through a major platform migration. The product will be in a degraded state for 3-6 months during the transition. Customers are worried. Your team is exhausted.

options.text: Create a customer advisory board — give your top customers a direct line to the migration team. Their feedback will keep you honest and their buy-in will keep them loyal.
Break the migration into weekly milestones with visible progress. The team needs wins, and customers need to see momentum. Cadence is everything.
Use this as the inflection point to leap ahead of competitors — design the new platform around the future, not as a replica of the past.
Set up comprehensive monitoring and rollback capabilities — instrument everything so you can detect regressions instantly and protect the customer experience with data.

questions.scenario: After years of building, your product has achieved a dominant market position. Growth is decelerating naturally. The question at the all-hands is: what's next?

options.text: Invest in adjacent markets — use your distribution advantage to expand into complementary products. The platform play is the endgame.
Go deeper, not wider. The best moat is an experience so good that switching costs are emotional, not just practical. Polish everything.
Bet on the next technology paradigm — AI, spatial computing, whatever comes next. Dominant positions are disrupted by platform shifts, not competitors.
Invest in your people and culture — the next chapter will be written by the team you build. Focus on attracting world-class talent who see the next opportunity.
